I believe 1406 BC is the correct starting point for the Jubilee count.

Here’s why:
	•	Joshua 5:10–12 shows Israel kept Passover right after crossing the Jordan in 1406 BC — this is when they “came into the land” (Lev 25:2).
	•	That means the Sabbatical and Jubilee cycle should start then, not years later.
	•	Counting 49-year cycles forward from 1406 BC gives 70 Jubilees landing in AD 2025 — the 70th Jubilee, a once-in-history prophetic milestone.

And here’s the amazing part: because this is a Jubilee year, the Feast of Trumpets is pushed forward to October 3 — aligning with the Day of Atonement! On this single day, three prophetic events come together:
	•	Feast of Trumpets – “the day no man knows the day or hour,” the trumpet call announcing the King.
	•	Day of Atonement – the day of cleansing, repentance, and restoration.
	•	Jubilee Trumpet – the great shofar proclaiming liberty and every person returning to their inheritance (Lev 25:9–10).

This is not just another feast day — this is Trumpets, Atonement, and Jubilee all rolled into one, pointing to freedom, redemption, and the open door of heaven (Rev 4:1). If there was ever a perfect picture of the rapture — the trumpet blast, the call to “come up here,” and the restoration of all things — this is it.

Be ready. Be watching. This could be the day we’ve been waiting for.

Author: @MindoftheInfinite
Content:
You’re not wrong you just don’t know what you’re looking at. The “rapture” isn’t about disappearing into the sky, but about an unveiling. In Greek, the word means to be caught up, seized, or revealed — it’s less about escape and more about what is exposed. When the so-called prediction didn’t happen in the way people expected, the real unveiling happened in the reactions. Some mocked, some denied with surface explanations, and some stayed sober, patient, and watchful. Their own words revealed their hearts. That unveiling itself is God’s doing, because God works through us. If God is infinite, then even denial still unfolds within God. Faith reveals God by accepting, denial reveals God by resisting, but both responses testify to the truth being made visible. So the rapture isn’t about running from the world, but about reality itself being revealed — and each of us chooses how to respond to what is unveiled.

Had ai rewrite my tree into a comment.

Tree: The “rapture” and the unveiling (tree format)
	•	Not escape, but unveiling
	•	In Greek, the word means to be caught up / seized / revealed.
	•	It’s not mainly about vanishing into the sky, but about what is being exposed.
	•	The so-called failed prediction
	•	The date passed, and nothing “spectacular” happened.
	•	But the real event was in the comments: how people reacted.
	•	That reaction itself became the unveiling.
	•	What was revealed
	•	Some mocked and dismissed.
	•	Some denied and explained it away on the surface.
	•	Some stayed sober, patient, and watchful.
	•	Each response showed the heart behind it.
	•	God’s doing through us
	•	God works through human choices, words, and actions.
	•	By their own words, people revealed where they stood.
	•	Faith and denial both became part of the unveiling.
	•	The infinite reality
	•	If God is infinite, then even denial unfolds within God.
	•	Faith reveals God by accepting.
	•	Denial reveals God by resisting.
	•	Nothing stands outside the infinite — even what we reject still testifies.
	•	The meaning
	•	The “rapture” is not about running away from the world.
	•	It is about seeing reality exposed for what it is.
	•	What was hidden is now made visible.
	•	The choice is in how we respond to what is revealed.

Author: @AmandaChen-n8d6g
Content:
The rapture is a belief mainly in certain branches of Christianity, especially in some Protestant evangelical traditions. It teaches that before the end of the world, true believers will suddenly be taken up (“raptured”) into heaven, leaving everyone else behind to face a period of suffering.

Here’s why many people (including other Christians, historians, and scholars) consider it fake news or not literally real:


---

1. No Clear Biblical Basis

The word rapture never appears in the Bible.

The main verses often cited (like 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 or Matthew 24:40–41) don’t describe the detailed scenario modern preachers talk about.

The “rapture” as popularly taught is more of an interpretation, not a direct biblical teaching.



---

2. A Very Recent Idea

For most of Christian history (about 1,800 years), no one taught the rapture.

It became popular in the 1800s through John Nelson Darby (an English preacher) and then spread in the U.S. through books and TV evangelists.

That’s why many traditional churches (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, etc.) reject it as unbiblical.



---

3. Fear and Profit

Rapture preaching is often tied to fear-based religion—warning people the end is coming soon.

Books like Left Behind and TV shows made millions off this idea, but that doesn’t make it true.

Fear of “being left behind” is used to control behavior and sell products, not to prove facts.



---

4. No Evidence in Reality

Predictions of the rapture have been made many times (e.g., 1988, 2000, 2011, etc.) and always failed.

If it were real in the literal sense, at least one of those predictions should have come true.

What does happen is natural disasters, wars, and social changes—which people misinterpret as “signs.”



---

5. Alternative Explanations

Many Christian theologians see the verses as symbolic: “meeting Christ in the air” is about ultimate union with God, not a sci-fi style disappearance.

Others say it’s a metaphor for hope and renewal, not an event where cars crash because drivers vanish.



---

✅ Bottom line: The rapture is considered “fake news” because it’s a modern invention, not taught in early Christianity, has no hard evidence, and is fueled by fear and media hype rather than history or scripture.
